pm_exper_user_3476_maasv_v0446_pmv2_r1.all_options:
(a) Given your recent struggle to write compelling features, you could borrow from your own journalistic recovery methods—say, engaging in conversations with local artists or academics, but this time photographing the exchanges rather than quoting them. Shifting the focus from the pressure of ‘getting the shot’ to capturing human moments might restore your ability to see stories in images.
(b) If your photography feels uninspired, try assigning yourself a small, unusual project—perhaps documenting a single colour, texture, or light source over several days. By narrowing the focus and committing to a playful experiment, you can trick your creative mind into noticing beauty in the ordinary again.
(c) Since you’ve just come through a creative block that stalled your feature writing, it might help to approach photography the way you’d approach a stalled article: set yourself a tightly defined, almost arbitrary brief—such as documenting one unnoticed cultural detail in Shoreditch each day—and treat it as reportage rather than pure art. The discipline of a small daily mission can rekindle both your visual eye and narrative instinct.
(d) When you were wrestling with that months-long block in your feature writing, revisiting old notes and unearthing overlooked drafts helped you find threads worth following. Apply that to photography: return to your old photo archives, linger over forgotten frames, and re-edit them—you may discover recurring themes or moods that inspire new work out in the field.
